<reason>A tight, well-matched debate. CON's strongest move was the "such as" scope argument plus the closing tally that PRO's complaints all target a "headline," and the motion's verb is "stop using." But PRO answered the scope question directly (the "because" clause scopes the target), turned the publisher question well (admission against interest vs. advertising), and made the decisive practical point stick: MBTI and DISC as actually sold and deployed ARE the letters — the workshop is named after them, the mug says INTJ — so CON's "keep using them but ignore the letter" is a defence of a different product. CON never showed that DISC/MBTI's underlying scales themselves predict performance; it borrowed conscientiousness/Big Five credibility that PRO explicitly exempted, and PRO called that out ("DISC borrowing credibility from a measure it isn't"). CON's convenience point ([B2.8]) was partly turned into "the market runs on convenience, not validity." Two clipped CON turns are a minor execution cost. PRO's asymmetry weighing (modest conversational upside that needs no test vs. a durable sticky label only a test creates) gave the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1/A5 sequence: after CON answered "yes, keep using them, ignore the letter" [B4.1], PRO framed this as conceding the motion with a face-saving clause — nobody buys DISC for the intensity graph, the letter is the product — which neutralized CON's "stop using vs. drop the codes" distinction better than CON's headline reframe neutralized PRO's harms.</best_rebuttal>
